classification.difficultyReason: Use the explicitly taught compound-angle substitution, transform the domain, enumerate all relevant exact-angle solutions and map back to x. Supplied curves scaffold the final interpretation as intersections with a horizontal line.

content.prompt: Solve each equation algebraically in the domain $[0,2\pi]$ and indicate the solutions on the graph.

spec.description: Sine curve with filled endpoints, labelled axes and quarter-period labels; unlabelled horizontal ticks occur every pi/6. No grid.
spec.answerVisibility: Curve and axes supplied; solution markings hidden.

answer.worked:
Let $u=x-\frac{\pi}{3}$. The transformed domain is $-\frac{\pi}{3}\le u\le\frac{5\pi}{3}$.
$$\begin{align*}2\sin u&=1\\\sin u&=\frac12\\u&=\frac{\pi}{6},\ \frac{5\pi}{6}\\x&=u+\frac{\pi}{3}\\x&=\frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{7\pi}{6}.\end{align*}$$
Draw $y=1$ and mark its intersections with the supplied curve.

spec.description: Solution overlay uses the identical coordinate units and bounding box as the question graph. A dashed horizontal line and marked intersections indicate both solutions.

answer.worked:
Let $u=2x$. The transformed domain is $0\le u\le4\pi$.
$$\begin{align*}2\cos u&=-1\\\cos u&=-\frac12\\u&=\frac{2\pi}{3},\ \frac{4\pi}{3},\ \frac{8\pi}{3},\ \frac{10\pi}{3}\\x&=\frac{u}{2}\\x&=\frac{\pi}{3},\ \frac{2\pi}{3},\ \frac{4\pi}{3},\ \frac{5\pi}{3}.\end{align*}$$
Draw $y=-1$ and mark its four intersections with the supplied curve.

spec.description: Solution overlay uses the identical coordinate units and bounding box as the question graph. A dashed horizontal line and marked intersections indicate all four solutions.
